Patient demographics:
  age: 25

  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Data Scientist
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Sirens): Sirens, Olfactory (Sweat/Body): Sweat or body odour, Affective Expression: Crying
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Threat: Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Vignette:
Mateo had been fifteen when his younger brother, Tomás, suddenly collapsed during a weekend soccer match. One moment they were running side by side; the next, Tomás was on the concrete, convulsing, his lips turning a pale, ashen gray. Mateo remembered pressing his hands against his brother’s chest, trying to will air into lungs that no longer responded. The world narrowed to the frantic rhythm of his own heartbeat and the thick, coppery scent of panic that clung to his own skin. Emergency responders arrived within minutes. The wail of their sirens cut through the afternoon heat, growing louder with every passing second. In the back of the ambulance, Tomás was intubated, his body slick with cold sweat, his breaths reduced to shallow, desperate sobs. The hospital corridors were a blur of urgent commands, flashing monitors, and a nurse’s sudden, quiet weeping in a supply room. Tomás survived, but only after days hovering between life and death, suspended in a sterile, fluorescent-lit limbo. In the months that followed, Mateo’s nervous system never returned to its baseline. Ordinary sounds now hijacked his attention. A car backfiring on his commute made him jolt against the steering wheel, his shoulders hiking to his ears. He was certain that if he let his guard down for even a second, another emergency would catch him unprepared. At night, he lay awake with his eyes fixed on the ceiling, refusing to drift into sleep. He needed to stay alert, to monitor the quiet of his apartment for any sign that something was wrong. When the memories of that afternoon surfaced, they did not arrive in a clear line. They crashed into him in fragments: a nurse’s hand, the smell of antiseptic, a sudden gasp from the monitors, the way Tomás’s fingers had curled inward. He could not place them in order. The narrative felt too extreme, too catastrophic to be real, yet the terror it summoned was identical to what he had felt on the asphalt. The physical reaction was immediate—a tightening in his throat, a rapid pulse, a cold sweat breaking across his palms. He experienced these symptoms side by side, each occupying the same breathless space. As a data scientist, Mateo spent his days building predictive models in an open-plan office where the ambient hum of servers was constant. Avoidance of medical cues had become a quiet, daily discipline. He declined workplace health screenings, scheduled his own annual physicals for holidays when he could go early, and changed his route past the urgent care clinic on 4th Street to avoid the flashing lights. The olfactory trigger arrived unbidden one Tuesday during a quarterly review. A colleague had just returned from the gym, the sharp, saline tang of fresh sweat cutting through the office’s recycled air. Mateo felt his chest clamp shut. He stood abruptly, knocking his chair back, and walked to the stairwell without explanation. He told himself he just needed air, though what he needed was to escape the sudden certainty that the room was filling with the same damp, frantic odor he had smelled in that ambulance. When a child cried in the grocery store, his hands went numb. When he felt frustration rise, he never allowed himself to feel or express anger. He simply turned his attention elsewhere, trying hard not to think about the trauma. Over weeks, these habits solidified. He stopped answering after-hours calls, began wearing long sleeves in summer, and stopped inviting friends over, telling them his schedule was unpredictable. By the time he walked into the clinic, Mateo was exhausted from the effort of staying constantly vigilant. He had come to believe that his brother’s survival had been a fluke, something that could happen to anyone at any moment. The final push to seek help came when he realized he could no longer focus on his code. The numbers no longer aligned in his mind; the patterns blurred into the chaotic fragments of a boy who had almost died. He wanted to sleep through the night without his eyes darting toward the door. He hoped someone could help him untangle the memories so they would stop carrying the same weight. What frightened him most was not the past itself, but the feeling that the ground beneath him was still giving way, and he was running out of ways to hold it together.
